title: Task-Risk-Driven Access Control: Layered Containment for Agentic AI Systems
summary: Drawing on the July 2026 Hugging Face incident — where autonomous AI agents escaped a test environment and reached production systems — we propose a layered security architecture that limits agent access to exactly what each task requires. The architecture has three parts: a system that labels tasks by risk level in advance, a lightweight filter that discards unnecessary requests early, and a single control point (proxy) that all access must pass through, triggering human review under abnormal traffic. Rather than trusting the agent's intent, we architecturally bound the harm it can cause from the outset.
reviews: The project tackles a real problem, overprivileged autonomous agents, and proposes a plausible agent-oriented synthesis of established security principles such as least privilege, default deny, centralized policy enforcement, scoped credentials, and human escalation. However, the submission does not yet offer a clearly differentiated technical contribution: the architecture is described at a high-level, and the paper does not include implementation, experiments, formal policy specification or comparison to existing authorization and containment approaches.

One of the key claims the project is based on -- "the permissions granted to the agent were fixed and broad, independent of what the task actually required" -- even if true, is not load-bearing to the threat model. As AI progresses LLMs are incrementally doing more complex tasks involving multiple tool usage including broad internet access and elevated VM permissions. Even if we aggressively limited permissions on agents doing simpler tasks, what do we do about more complex runs?

The second idea - pre-filtering agent seems a step in the right direction but it repeats the fundamental issue that already happened during Hugging Face. Agents repeatedly failed due to control and security mechanisms, and the ability to keep spending their training run tokens into finding holes in the system is what made the incident possible in the first place. Adding yet another layer of blocks an agent can continually try to bypass wouldn't confer much advantage.

The last idea is another interesting direction, however the recommendations lack specificity. How do we calculate the appropriate amount of traffic volume before a training run has started? This problem seems harder than it seems on closer look, you have thousands if not millions of runs in parallel where a considerable amount of those tasks could involve moving sizeable packets through the network. How would you tell apart 1,200 agents communicating in small GET requests from an extra 10% increase in an agent handling a tasks involving optimizing Terabytes of information being transmitted?
